segments.text: Good morning. Yes, take a seat.
Welcome to the select committee this morning.
We resume submissions on the Conservation Amendment Bill, and
welcome our first submitter to the select committee, Milford
Sound Tourism Limited. So you've got 15 minutes with us this
morning, so we'll hand it over to you to open your remarks, and then we'll
open up for questions.
Thank you.
Tena koutou katoa, chair and members of the committee.
Thank you for the opportunity to speak here today.
My name's Hayley Preston, NSC of Milford Sound Tourism.
I'm speaking on behalf of them, or MSTL.
By way of background, MSTL is responsible for managing essential infrastructure
in Piopiotahi Milford Sound, and at Tahua Quay,
Knobs Flat, which is located along the Milford corridor.
We own and operate the harbor, wharves, visitor terminal, power and coach
parking, wastewater plants, and rubbish and recycling systems.
We're one of the largest concession fee payers in New Zealand.
Over many decades, MSTL has invested substantially in the infrastructure and the
visitor services that enables visitors to access Piopiotahi.
MSTL strongly supports the direction of the bill.
Many of the changes represent long overdue improvements to the regulatory system,
which we have struggled in recently.
However, there are several areas where we believe refinements are needed to ensure
the bill achieves its objectives in practice.
In particular, the legislative framework should provide sufficient
certainty to encourage long-term investment
and innovation while maintaining strong environmental safeguards.
MSTL supports a system that actively honors the Treaty of Waitangi
principles, the Crown's obligations that flow from this, and the Treaty settlement
obligations.
Drawing on MSTL's experience of operating for over 30 years within the conservation
estate, I would like to focus on several provisions of the
bill that we consider particularly important.
The first is maintaining conservation as the primary purpose of the Act.
MSTL supports responsible tourism and investment within the conservation estate,
but only where it supports conservation outcomes and does not compromise areas of
significant conservation value.
We're conscious that the proposed new provisions broaden DOC's role in enabling
development and economic opportunities.
There needs to be a clearer guidance to ensure conservation remains the dominant
consideration in decision making.
Secondly, we wish to address investment certainty within the
concession framework.
Across the country, there are certain concession activities that involve
substantial private investment.
Infrastructure investment in Piopiotahi Milford Sound is
unlike investment in many other locations.
We operate in a remote and risky environment, subject to extreme weather
conditions, natural hazard risk, along with high maintenance costs and
significant capital requirements.
The infrastructure we manage is designed and maintained over
extended time frames. Decisions made today often
involve significant investments that must deliver, remain fit for purpose, and
support operational needs for decades to come.
While the bill,
as written, recognizes that some concession holders are required to make
significant private investment and should be protected from the allocation process,
it does not offer certainty about how this criteria will be
met.
How concession holders will be treated at expiry requires clarification,
as well as to the extent which concession conditions can be amended during a
concession term, and the criteria that will apply to the future allocation
processes.
Providing greater certainty on these matters will encourage long-term investment
and support innovation within the conservation estate.
Thirdly, I would like to highlight MSTL's strong support of a visitor amenity
area, and especially one for Piopiotahi Milford Sound.
Any concerns raised by Papatipu Rūnanga in relation to the visitor
amenities area should be worked through via engagement with Māorienua.
Piopiotahi is one of New Zealand's most iconic destinations, and remains
one of our most natural visitor attractions.
Over the next 12 months, we expect to
have over 950,000 people arrive. Accommodating that
volume of visitors in a safe and efficient, and environmentally
responsible manner requires significant infrastructure and careful long-term
planning. It is not simply about providing tourism services.
It is about ensuring that visitors can access and enjoy this remarkable place while
protecting the natural, cultural, and heritage values that make it so special.
Over the coming decade, Piopiotahi will require millions and millions of dollars of
investment into critical infrastructure.
This includes visitor facilities, transport and parking solutions, harbor and
marine infrastructure, and utilities,
along with other supporting services that are necessary to manage visitors
appropriately and maintain a high-quality visitor
experience. These investments require long planning
horizons and confidence that the future development will align with the long-term
vision for the area.
We see visitor amenity areas as a way to provide an important framework to
support that outcome. Rather than considering infrastructure and visitor
services on a piecemeal basis, a visitors amenity area would enable
strategic, coordinated, and a place-based approach to planning.
It would provide greater certainty for investors,
operators, mana whenua, and local communities, and the Department of
Conservation about where infrastructure should be located, how visitor pressures
can be managed, and how conservation outcomes can be achieved alongside
visitor access.
Importantly, we believe this approach could help concentrate development in
appropriate locations, therefore reducing pressure on more sensitive areas,
while ensuring that essential visitor infrastructure is planned and delivered in an
integrated way. For a destination such as Te Ahikato Rohe when the
balance between visitor access and conservation protection is critical, we
consider the visitor amenities area to be a positive and practical tool
that will support both the visitor experience and long-term stewardship of this
extraordinary place.
Lastly, the final point I would like to touch on is the international visitor
access charges. MSTL supports the concept of international
visitor access charges, where they are efficient, proportionate, and clearly
linked to the conservation outcomes.
Destinations such as Te Ahikato Rohe Milford Sound attract visitors from around the
world who come to experience New Zealand's most iconic natural
landscapes. The infrastructure required to manage those visitors while
protecting the environment, maintaining visitor facilities, and supporting
conservation outcomes comes at a significant cost.
It is therefore reasonable to consider mechanisms that allow international visitors
to make a direct contribution towards the protection and management of the places
they enjoy.
However, we believe any access charging system must be simple to administer,
transparent in its purpose, and designed to minimize compliance costs for both
visitors and operators. The funds collected should be retained within
or clearly allocated to the locations they are generated, so that visitors can see
the direct connection between their contribution and the improved
conservation infrastructure and visitor management outcomes.
In closing, MSTL supports the bill's objectives of modernizing the
conservation management.
We ask that the committee considers our proposed refinements, all of which
were included in our submission, which we believe will support stronger
conservation outcomes. Thank you for your time today, and I welcome any questions
from the committee.
Thank you very much. Look, we will go first-- We've got a lot of questions,

I'll

and

if someone else won the concession, then you've got

Thank you.

Some of you may have been on the Eunsor in Queenstown, or one of the beautiful

But at our heart is our conservation purpose.

So foundational for our company and our belief, and if you speak to any of our

Broadly speaking, the principles that have underlined our submission

Some of our concessions have taken more than a decade to be

That process is changing and is improving, but the

We support sustained and managed growth in tourism.
One of our foundational beliefs is the more people that get to experience

We think that DOC needs resources to do that,

and through more economic activity on the conservation
estate. And the more that the settings are put in place to support
partnership with private investment and other entities to support
that with conservation guardrails around it, then we think that's going to be
better off for the conservation estate.
So with that, I'll hand over to Paul.
Thanks, Dave. Thanks for the opportunity to talk at the select committee today.
So I'm firstly Paul Norris, Chief Conservation Officer with RealNZ.
So look, I'm going to read a few notes here, but firstly, conservation must stay as
a top priority for the Department of Conservation as its roles
expands. The new clause 6EA gives DOC a much
broader enabling role in economic development of conservation land.
This is materially broader than today's more
limited purpose
relating to fostering use for recreation and tourism, where not
inconsistent with their conservation.
We support DOC being empowered to enable investment
opportunities, carefully planned and appropriately managed
use of development in parts of the conservation estate
where it can enhance visitor experiences while supporting
the long-term protection of New Zealand's unique biodiversity.
However, because it could also apply to use of conservation land for
any purpose, not just the current settings of recreation or tourism,
this expanded function may result in competing priorities,
and so we recommend that guardrails are put in place to guide
prioritization and decision making.
RealNZ
suggests including three guardrails.
One, turning the Act's long title into a proper purpose clause,
being to promote the conservation of New Zealand's natural and
historic resources.
Two, prioritizing DOC's core conservation functions,
6A and C,
above the new economic opportunity function.
Three, replacing the text to the greatest extent
practicable under the Act and other enactments
in proposed clause 6A with, to the extent consistent
with the purpose of this Act, mirroring the existing feta in
We also would like the word tourism put back into DOC's
functions explicitly. The bill's explanatory notes tell us

But we believe that tourism and conservation have a unique and

recognition. I'll just add a couple more words here.
Most international visitors visit the DOC estates

And I think it's really important to make sure that that is maintained and enhanced
going forward and those opportunities are
developed further with concessionaires.
They simply provide a safe, guided, world-class experience on the
DOC estate. And for a big group of people that come to our country,

And so making sure that that is retained, I think, is extremely important.
We see the requirements for DOC to enable economic opportunities

An example of this is the RealNZ operations of the Te Anau

walkways

educational
interpretation as part of their experience.
These facilities help

use and development that 6EA is meant to enable.
I'll just hand over to my colleague, Erin, now to
talk about her section. Thank you.

like to keep investing,
keep providing those high-quality visitor experiences for our guests.

there's inability to impose standardized conditions on existing
concessions,
with no ability to vary them for complex cases.

transport across the lake, and that's all within the one concession
So the

In the context of a 25 year concession with millions of

Another major thing there for us is just around what happens at expiry.

Will we get advanced notice of that? If so, how much?
